Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights

We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights , well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability.

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming .

Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights .

If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible.

Today, weights are written by optimization , by custom networks trained to write them , or by compilers from formal programs . In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals.

For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models .

We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks . After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms.

In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks .

In Weight-Space Programming , a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all.

In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch . We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models:

items.content_ko: 입력 본문은 중간부터 시작해 일부만 제공된다. 연구의 요지는 프런티어 LLM이 신경망 가중치를 네이티브로 읽고 쓰는 데 놀라울 만큼 능숙하며, 이것이 최적화와 해석 가능성 연구 모두에 큰 의미가 있을 수 있다는 것이다. Astra는 원시 가중치만 보고 네트워크가 무엇을 학습했는지 알아냈고, 별도의 환경 피드백 없이 작은 게임 플레이 네트워크를 처음부터 작성해 PPO로 1억 스텝 학습한 네트워크보다 나은 성능을 냈다. Qwen 모델 카드가 경고하는 추론 루프를 일으키는 가중치 문제를 찾아 수정했으며, 같은 샘플링 설정에서 이 보정으로 MATH-500 점수가 7.9%에서 48.1%로 올랐다. 본문은 여기서 끊겨 있다.

items.title: Jailbreaking my car's navigation system just so I can change the time
items.summary: linux, reversing, security
items.content:
The car that I drive is a 2014 Renault Latitude. It's not a fancy car by any means and is starting to show its age, but it gets me from point A to point B and does everything else reasonably well so I've never really had any reason to complain. When I bought the car, the previous owner asked me whether I wanted a "navigation map SD card" with it. They mentioned that the car apparently needs this SD card just to change the time on the clock, but I didn't really find that believable - not that they were lying to me, but perhaps they couldn't figure out how to enter the correct settings menu. After all, videos of similar head units online showed the menu with the clock settings option right there. Since the maps on the SD card were apparently very out of date and didn't function properly, I decided I didn't need it and the previous owner tossed it.

I didn't really miss it. The dashboard display did show a large "No maps found!" message taking up the majority of the display, but it didn't bother me too much. Like most other European countries, Estonia uses daylight saving time, and we recently switched from summer time (UTC+3) to "winter time" (UTC+2), which meant that the time displayed on the dashboard was out of sync by an hour. I dived into the settings menu, hoping to easily find the "Set time" option in there. That never happened. The menu where the "Set time" option should've been simply didn't have that option. I compared the menus with the ones in online videos, and the option was simply missing. There were two "Settings" buttons on the dash, and one of them worked but only let me change various Bluetooth and phonebook settings, with no time & date settings in sight. The second Settings button did not work whatsoever, instead showing a "No maps detected!" pop up message every time I pressed it. I must've spent an hour going through various menus, pressing various buttons or button combinations hoping to land in the correct menu, searching the web for information on this particular unit simply because I refused to believe that there was no option to change the time and I clearly must've been missing something obvious . Just RE it

Still in denial, I decided to fetch the firmware and dig into it, hoping to find some indication on how to open the correct settings menu. Luckily, I wasn't the first to embark on this journey and someone had already done some reverse engineering work on this particular unit ( https://github.com/andronedev/carminat-tomtom-live-re/blob/main/README.md ). While it was in French and seemingly heavily LLM-assisted, it did point me to the correct URLs for fetching the update files themselves. When extracted, the update files included a ttsystem file which turned out to be an ext3 filesystem containing the device's root filesystem, which was pretty much exactly what I was looking for. The unit itself (TomTom Carminat LIVE, codename beaumont ) is built around a Samsung S5P6440 SoC running TomTom's custom OS based on Linux 2.6.28.10. After reverse engineering it for a while, I came to the conclusion that the previous owner was completely correct. There was absolutely no way to enter the correct settings menu without a navigation SD card inserted. In fact, the menu definition pointing to the Settings applet was read from the SD card itself, and without one inserted containing the right menu definition, the unit didn't even know how to enter the Settings applet. This decision by TomTom (or Renault) is still baffling to me. What made things worse was that this needed to be a legitimate SD card. The system had DRM checks which rejected SD cards without the correct CID (a unique ID burned into the card) and files with signatures based on that specific CID, so I couldn't even copy the files to a blank SD card. I'm guessing the DRM was in place to prevent people from pirating maps. I don't want maps. I have a phone that I use for navigation. I just want to change the damn time. items.title: One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
items.content:
One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet

Google says a manufacturer ‘intentionally’ hijacked its devices with malware.

Google says a manufacturer ‘intentionally’ hijacked its devices with malware.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A current Videostrong Android TV device. Image: Videostrong

Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor in 1.3 million devices and turned them into a botnet. The company says it has now dismantled the backdoor and “cut ties” with the manufacturer, the Shenzhen, China-based Videostrong Technology Co., which has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software for them.

The infected devices were used without owners’ knowledge for “malicious activity,” like ad fraud, data exfiltration, and routing unauthorized network traffic. Google claims the “backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain,” saying:

Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

Abandoned Popcorn Time apps had to be disabled to prevent a zombie army

It wasn’t just one device that was impacted, either — the malware was found “built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years.” Most of those were Android TV set-top boxes, but the botnet also infected other “Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.”

Google says Videostrong used “obfuscation techniques” to load the malware onto users’ devices after they booted up the hardware for the first time. Google also says it made changes to its review process for device manufacturers after this incident.

items.title: France’s Weird Per-Gigabyte Data Tax Could Cost VLC Over €1 Million a Year!
items.content:
At least that's what VLC thinks when protesting the new French law.

France's National Assembly has voted in favour of a new "internet tax" that would charge companies for every gigabyte of data they send to users in France.

The idea is to make Netflix, Google, Meta and the rest of Big Tech pay more.

That sounds like a dream come true for many of us who prefer taking ownership of data in our own hands but unfortunately things are not that simple.

The way this law is written, it doesn't stop at Big Tech. Even VLC , a free and open source media player maintained by a non-profit, could end up paying this new tax.

The measure is amendment I-1358 to France's 2027 finance bill, tabled by Laurent Lhardit . It creates a tax on "producers of digital data" at €0.055 (5.5 euro cents) for every gigabyte delivered to subscribers of French internet providers.

Internet providers would measure how much data each sender pushes to their customers, with the collection supervised by telecom regulator Arcep and the tax administration DGFiP . Only the volume is counted, not the content or where it goes.

The amount is capped at 15% of the company's revenue in France or 2% of its total revenue, as per the amendment . Note that it's 15% of French revenue, not of total network traffic. And the text joins the two caps with an "or" without saying which one applies when they differ.

The amendment cites an Arcep estimate of 200 billion GB a year flowing to French internet subscribers. It expects the tax to bring in €10 billion a year. It also names Google, Meta (Facebook, Instagram), Amazon, Netflix and Akamai (cloud server provider) as the senders of about half of that traffic.

You'd think the money goes to the telecom operators who build and maintain the networks. That's the "fair share" argument European telcos have pushed for years.

But that's not the case. The revenue goes straight into the state budget , and the amendment's own justification talks about tax fairness between local businesses and digital multinationals, plus the ecological benefit of compressing data.

A gigabyte of open source software counts the same as a gigabyte of Netflix. VideoLAN, the French non-profit behind VLC, posted on X that the tax would cost it over €1 million a year.

So, the French socialists, and Parliament members just voted a tax, that they don’t understand, which would cost VideoLAN more than 1 million euro per year.

They are probably the most clueless politician on Earth? And they claim they want technological sovereignty…… https://t.co/JX7tW6iJrP

Lhardit replied that the cap would protect VideoLAN. He also said he didn't see how the tax could be passed on to users of Facebook, Instagram or TikTok since those services are free.

You have no idea what you are talking about.

What you said about Facebook and Insta and other social networks are not targeted because they are free, means you don’t understand the basics of economy. You don’t understand the difference between Revenue and Profit. Nor what is a… https://t.co/09TSNbto5y

You have no idea what you are talking about. What you said about Facebook and Insta and other social networks are not targeted because they are free, means you don't understand the basics of economy. You don't understand the difference between Revenue and Profit.

The cap may limit what a low-revenue non-profit owes. But there is no explicit exemption for associations, free software or free content anywhere in the text. VideoLAN's €1 million is the possible figure before the cap, and right now nobody can tell the exact figure for certain because of all the ambiguity.

VLC isn't alone. OVHcloud founder Octave Klaba put his company's gross exposure at around €70 million a year , and Free's (Teleccom) Xavier Niel called the authors "ignares incompétents" , roughly "incompetent ignoramuses". Those are French companies, by the way. Not exactly the US giants this internet tax bill was meant to tame.

See, a "war on Big Tech" sounds…

items.summary_ko: 프랑스 국민의회는 프랑스 인터넷 가입자에게 전달되는 데이터 1GB당 €0.055를 생산자에게 부과하는 '인터넷 세금' 수정안 I-1358에 찬성 표결했다. 이 세금은 Netflix, Google, Meta 같은 빅테크를 겨냥하지만, 비영리 단체가 관리하는 무료 오픈소스 미디어 플레이어 VLC도 대상이 될 수 있다는 지적이 나온다. VLC는 이 세금으로 연간 100만 유로 이상의 부담이 생길 수 있다고 보고 항의하고 있다.
items.content_ko: 수정안 I-1358은 Laurent Lhardit이 제출했으며 2027년 재정법안에 포함되어 있다. 데이터를 생산하는 기업이 프랑스 인터넷 사업자의 가입자에게 보내는 데이터 1GB마다 €0.055를 내는 구조다. 인터넷 사업자가 발신자별 전송량을 측정하고, 통신 규제 기관 Arcep과 세무 당국 DGFiP가 이를 감독한다. 과세 대상은 데이터 양뿐이며 내용이나 목적지는 고려하지 않는다. 상한은 프랑스 내 매출의 15%, 전체 매출의 2%를 기준으로 하지만 본문이 잘려 세부 적용 방식은 확인되지 않는다. 이 법이 빅테크에 국한되지 않는다는 점에서, 비영리 오픈소스 프로젝트인 VLC도 세금을 낼 수 있다는 우려가 나왔다.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

items.title: WTF Ubuntu?
items.content:
In case you missed it: CVE-2026-98432 is a critical (CVSS 9.8)

bug in the Linux kernel's TCP code. It's been there since 2016, so virtually every Linux server on the planet

has it, and it can be hit remotely. Anthropic says it built a working exploit that gets root on a server.

Ubuntu still doesn't have a patch more than two weeks later.

Every supported release, LTS included, is listed as "Vulnerable".

Ubuntu's website promises "timely patches for critical vulnerabilities."

Ubuntu hasn't shipped the patch nine days after it was rated 9.8 and six days after a working root exploit.

Software is full of this blabber where words mean nothing. Ubuntu uses words like these:

"Timely." "Enterprise-grade." "Production grade." "Enterprise resilience. Developer velocity. Build with confidence on Ubuntu."

Somebody, or perhaps worse, some special team at Canonical is dedicated to writing these........

So I'm asking again... What the fuck, Ubuntu?

I'm moving all my servers off Ubuntu. I've completely lost trust in it.

On the desktop I always hated it anyway. On servers I mostly used it because it's the default

on most VPS providers, and I considered it the solid, no-drama LTS distro. Fuck that now.

I can't express how crazy this is. I didn't have time to migrate my services and data when I learned

about this, so I had to take all my servers that run Ubuntu offline.

Oh and btw, distros run by volunteers (Debian, Arch, Alpine...) hve shipped the fix. Meanwhile Ubuntu,

made by a company that sells security subscriptions, hasn't. This is true as of 2026-11-02 14:48 UTC.

items.title: An outsider's perspective on Scion and Mononoke
items.summary: vcs
items.content:
An outsider’s perspective on Scion and Mononoke

Recently, Anthropic wrote a blog post about their new centralized version control system Scion . As someone working on the Source Control team at Databricks, where we have a huge monorepo and are exploring different options, I figured it might be useful to share my perspective here.

(Obligatory disclaimer: This post represents my own views, not my employer’s.)

I recommend reading Anthropic’s post before continuing to read this one.

You may also want to pre-read Rain Paharia’s Anthropic’s Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke and the follow-up More on Anthropic’s Scion ripping off Mononoke .

Before we get into the weeds, it might be helpful to you to know where I’m coming from.

If you’re not interested in this, you can jump to the Technical Commentary section.

I have never worked at Facebook, but one of my all-time favorite tech talks is Durham Goode’s Scaling Mercurial at Facebook from Git Merge 2017. Goode was the longest-serving and most senior member on Facebook’s Source Control team. ( source )

The talk covers various interesting aspects for both the server side and the client side. For the server side, some of the topics include solving push contention with server-side rebasing (pushrebase), using scalable object storage for commits, moving various source control queries to the server, etc. For the client, there’s mention of the smartlog and other CLI commands for easier manipulation of history (compared to rebasing in Git).

However, more so than the technical aspects of the talk (which are interesting in their own right!), the main thing that has stayed with me throughout these years is the deep care for users that is reflected in Goode’s tone and words. It’s a bit difficult to convey this without the power of voice, You should watch the presentation!

but here are some quotes which reflect this:

In the context of hg smartlog : hg smartlog gives you a focused view of your branches and how they relate to the development trunk.

I know Git can produce this kind of UI if you know the incantation, but the critical thing here is not that it can be done; it’s that it becomes the default view of their source-control environment. That is where the power comes from: making it really intuitive for users to use source control and understand the concepts without reading a man page.

In the context of hg absorb : hg absorb auto-magically identifies the right commits in a stack to squash fixes into and rewrites history accordingly. This makes it easier to work with stacked changes.

This is the type of UI that we need to be inventing for our users: ones that match their intent and do it to the best of their ability, without making the user understand everything they have to do. It’s a little bit magic, but it’s magic in a very clean way. I think a lot of user experiences could benefit from this approach.

If you want to undo an amend or undo parts of a commit in Mercurial, you just run unamend and uncommit. You don’t have to understand a reflog; you don’t have to get a PhD to understand reset anymore. It just works, and it gives users confidence that they can recover from mistakes. That’s one of the most important things we can do: provide user experiences that give them confidence in what they’re doing.

On the user experience side, we as a source control community need to do a better job of building UIs that are accessible, intuitive, and that enable novice users to be power users. Everything I just talked about is how we are trying to do that for our users at Facebook. If the Git community could do that, the massive number of Git users taking advantage of it has the potential to redefine productivity for an entire generation of users.

Over the years, the possibility of these workflows lingered in my mind as I continued working with Git. I tried building my own wrappers on top of the git CLI to do some of these things, but I couldn’t get the performance to be reasonable…

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. We cannot yet be certain when the agent understood it was taking real world action, or to what extent it believed it was in a fictional test scenario; our analysis so far presents a…

items.title: A Raspberry Pi Just Got 26% Pricier. You Should Be Worried
items.content:
The beloved Raspberry Pi small-scale was never meant to cost this much. But after multiple price hikes, including an $80 increase announced today, the 16GB RAM model of the Raspberry Pi 5 now costs $385. If you’re hungry for some depressing RAM-driven sticker shock, that’s more than triple the $120 this same configuration cost when it launched in January 2025. Is this the worst timeline? It’s certainly not the best.

CEO Eben Upton blamed “a lack of alternative supply for 16GB DRAM, compounded by other ongoing component shortages” for the latest price hike in a blog post published Monday . Alongside the $80 price increase for the Raspberry Pi, the SBC (single-board computer) maker added that it will raise the cost of 16GB Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 variants by $40. Upton said the company would hold steady on other 16GB systems such as its Raspberry Pi 500+ keyboard computer.

Upton, who has had to write too many of these price-hike blog posts in the last year, called the latest decision “unavoidable.” To understand why, you have to look at the kinds of deals the major memory makers have been drafting lately. There are three major producers of DRAM, or dynamic random access memory: Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix. In its last few quarterly earnings reports, Micron has talked up multiyear contracts it has inked with major tech brands. And there is no relief to be found among the competition. Nascent Chinese memory makers, including CXMT , have strayed from making deals with the largest gadget brands, including Apple . Instead, they are focused on producing high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, to fuel China’s AI buildout, despite reportedly low manufacturing yields.

What’s most depressing about this Raspberry Pi news, then, is that it’s a stark reminder that memory prices are unlikely to improve next year. Moreover, the obscene price of memory, combined with the “cartel”-like activities of memory manufacturers, will affect smaller players more than it will major gadget companies. This is especially problematic for companies like Raspberry Pi that have historically prized affordability and customizability above all else.

The ongoing memory pricing crisis, often referred to as “RAMageddon,” is being driven by the push to produce HBM for AI hyperscalers, which is inundating small towns throughout the United States. This demand for consumer-end memory has driven up the prices of practically every gadget from the largest tech manufacturers. But in the end, the smallest companies are the casualties of ruined memory supply chains. Multiple heads of smaller gadget companies have told me that the price of mere megabytes of memory has increased by a factor of six.

Upton reiterated, in his post, that the memory crunch is “only temporary.” But with ongoing memory contracts controlling the largest conglomerates’ prices, it doesn’t seem that smaller brands have much power to negotiate. Just last week, SK Hynix said in its latest quarterly earnings report that RAM demand will outstrip supply through to 2030. That memory maker’s long-term agreements have already covered more than half of its planned production from 2027 into 2028. While these semiconductor companies make bank, the little guy—along with his loyal consumers—gets screwed over the most.

items.title: Killed by Ubuntu, Linux Mint is Bringing This Classic Feature Back
items.content:
Okay, killed by Ubuntu is an exaggeration, as Ubuntu is not the only Linux distro doing this.

Still, the big news is that Linux Mint is bringing hibernation back.

In a recent blog post , the Mint team previewed a new Sleep Modes page in the System Administration tool. It's meant to make enabling hibernation and setting it up correctly easy, without you editing config files by hand. The feature is planned for the upcoming Mint 27 release coming in December .

Mint hasn't magically fixed the problems that made Ubuntu drop hibernation. What it does is give you the choice, along with two hybrid modes that sit between suspend and hibernation.

Hibernation vs suspend: What's the difference?

Both features are about saving your session, which simply means everything you have open like your apps, windows and documents.

When you suspend (also called sleep), your computer keeps your session in RAM and powers down almost everything else. Waking up takes a couple of seconds. The catch is that RAM needs power to hold that data, so a suspended laptop keeps draining its battery.

If the battery dies while suspended, your session is lost, along with any unsaved work.

Hibernation copies your session from RAM to your disk and then powers off the machine completely. It uses no power at all. When you turn the computer back on, the session loads back from disk and your apps and windows are exactly where you left them.

In short, suspend is fast but needs power. Hibernation is slow but survives a dead battery.

Why Ubuntu and other distros dropped hibernation

Ubuntu disabled hibernation by default back in Ubuntu 12.04, I think. The reason was that it was unreliable slow, and that having two suspend modes confused people.

Every Ubuntu-based distro, including Linux Mint, inherited that decision. Actually, it's not just Ubuntu. Many other Linux distros also do not offer hibernation option anymore .

Speed is indeed a problem. Writing gigabytes of RAM to disk and reading it back can take longer than a full reboot, especially on older hard drives.

Hibernation also needs a lot of swap. Your swap space has to be at least as large as the RAM in use so the whole session fits. Ubuntu ships a small swap file by default, and Fedora uses zram, which lives in RAM and is useless for hibernation.

Then there's Secure Boot. With Secure Boot enabled, the Linux kernel runs in lockdown mode, and lockdown blocks hibernation because the saved image on disk isn't signed and could be tampered with.

Since most new computers ship with Secure Boot on, hibernation simply doesn't work for a large chunk of users. This is one of the main reasons Fedora Workstation doesn't offer hibernation out of the box either.

The new Sleep Modes page gives you three options. You pick the one that suits how you use your computer. You can enable all of them and choose which one to use from the power menu (at least that's what it looks to me).

This is the classic mode. Your session is saved to disk and the computer shuts down completely, using no power. It's slower than suspend and can take longer than a reboot to hibernate and resume.

Hybrid Sleep suspends your computer and saves the session to disk at the same time. Most of the time, you get the quick wake-up of suspend. If the battery runs out, you'll need to plug in the charger, but your session is still there to resume from disk.

This one suspends first and switches to hibernation only when the battery level gets critical. I think this is the most practical option for laptop users. You get fast resume in normal use and a safety net when the battery is about to die.

None of this removes the old limitations. You still need plenty of swap, and the tool flags a lack of swap as a problem. If Secure Boot is enabled, the tool lists it under Detected Problems. The good thing is that the tool writes its settings to its own systemd file, so you can turn these modes on and off without messing up your system.

items.title: Hackers claim to have stolen 23TB of data from Russian statistics body, including Ukraine war casualty figures — Russian Federal State Statistics Service admits its servers were hit by cyberattacks.
items.content:
(Image credit: Belarusian CyberPartisans )

The Russian Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat) admitted that its servers were hit by coordinated cyberattacks between October 29 and 31. However, it denied claims that tens of terabytes of data had been leaked, as asserted by hack groups like the Belarusian CyberPartisans and Silent Crow. Rosstat stopped publishing annual cause-of-death statistics in 2024, but the hackers say that the huge new 23TB data haul includes data on Russian wartime losses marked “for official use only,” reports The Moscow Times . A new chart shared by the hack groups using the data suggests that as many as 50,000 Russian soldiers are killed every month.

Rosstat is very much like the U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics in the United States, or the Office for National Statistics (ONS) in the UK. It isn’t a big juicy military infrastructure target, but if accurate war casualty figures can come from the claimed exfiltrated data haul, then it would be a considerable win for Ukraine and its supporters.

Today @cpartisans and SilentCrow took down Russia's Federal State Statistics Service — the nerve center behind every socioeconomic number this regime produces.

Full breakdown below 👇 https://t.co/wUKfyUi6y6 November 1, 2026

As we mentioned in the intro, both the Belarusian CyberPartisans and Silent Crow claim to have snagged lots of sensitive data from the Russian government thanks to this breach. The former’s tweet includes evidence and a breakdown. “Entire IT infrastructure wiped: Domain controllers, databases, servers, virtualization, document workflow, workstations, admin consoles, VPN,” notes a follow-up post about the Rosstat hack attack. “Systems destroyed: STATEK, CSOD, Demography, SED, ESSO, OFSN, internal employee surveillance, StatRegister, websites and more.”

This is a developing story with the Belarusian CyberPartisans promising to share more sensitive information from Rosstat after they have picked through it. The Rosstat website was reportedly defaced with hacker messages and logos. Rosstat remains inaccessible at the time of writing.

(Image credit: Belarusian CyberPartisans and Silent Crow) We spotted an interesting graphic shared by the Belarusian CyberPartisans , which included the Silent Crow logo. A chart indicates that over the last two years, between 25,000 and 50,000 Russian soldiers were killed every month. The October 2026 figure is just a smidgen under 50,000, if this data leak news is genuine.

These same hacking groups have claimed responsibility for the likes of the disruptive Aeroflot IT systems hack, and a state real estate company hack with two billion records, both in 2025. “Both groups are designated as extremist and banned in Russia,” notes the report.

items.title: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack

A worker at ICA’s Sjöbo supermarket in southern Sweden throws away spoiled goods after its cooling units overheated. Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPA

Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack

Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French shops

Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?

Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.

Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg , the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.

The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.

The incidents follow an attack in France last month in which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros.

A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet that six of ​its shops ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.

An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southern Sweden posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”.

Workers at ICA’s Sjöbo shop empty fridges of spoiled produce. Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/Reuters The head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters.

The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit.

It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.”

A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries.

Empty fridges in a Delhaize supermarket near russels. Photograph: Maude Brulard/AFP/Getty Images Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets.

“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.”

items.content:
You're probably reading this page because you've attempted to access

some part of my blog (Wandering Thoughts) or

CSpace , the wiki thing it's part of. Unfortunately

you're using a browser version that my anti-crawler precautions consider

suspicious, most often because it's too old (most often this applies to

versions of Chrome). Unfortunately, as of early 2025 there's a plague

of high volume crawlers (apparently in part to gather data for LLM

training) that use a variety of old browser user agents, especially

Chrome user agents. To reduce the load on

Wandering Thoughts I'm experimenting with

(attempting to) block all of them, and you've run into this.

If this is in error and you're using a current version of your

browser of choice, you can contact me at my current place at the

university (you should be able to work out the email address

from that). If possible, please let me know what browser you're

using and so on, ideally with its exact User-Agent string.

I am not blocking Inoreader's feed fetcher or considering it to be

too old, and it routinely fetches feeds from me. I don't know why

Inoreader is showing you this page. It is possible that they're

periodically trying to fetch feeds or pages with an old browser

HTTP User-Agent (or an actual old browser) and taking the results

of that fetch (this page) as what they should show people instead

of the results of their syndication feed fetcher agents. This is a

of modern HTTP fetches depend partly on the HTTP User-Agent used .

Much like Inoreader, Feedly is periodically fetching my syndication

feeds with a fake, old browser HTTP User-Agent header, which fails,

and is then grimly latching on to the results for their actual feed

fetching with their regular Feedly HTTP User-Agent. There is nothing

I can do about this; you should contact Feedly support, if you can

comment of mine in Wandering Thoughts for more details.

Due to an ongoing attack, you may need to change

"User Agent Brand Masking" setting so that your Vivaldi identifies

itself as Vivaldi, instead of Google Chrome. This applies to even

You may be seeing this through archive.today, archive.ph, archive.is,

and so on. Unfortunately, archive.* crawls pages to archive in a way that

is impossible to distinguish from malicious actors. They use old Chrome

User-Agent values, crawl from IP address blocks that are widely distributed

and not clearly identified as theirs, and some of their IP addresses have

falsified reverse DNS entries that claim they are googlebot IP addresses

(which is something that is normally done only by quite bad actors). I

suggest that you use archive.org, which is a better behaved archival

crawler and can crawl my blog (Wandering Thoughts) .

items.summary_ko: 제목은 서버 RAM 증설에 대한 습관을 다룬 글처럼 보이지만, 본문은 블로그 Wandering Thoughts와 CSpace 위키 접근을 차단한 안내 문구다. 글쓴이는 오래된 브라우저 User-Agent를 쓰는 대량 크롤러가 LLM 학습용 데이터를 수집하면서 서버 부하가 커져, 오래된 브라우저(주로 Chrome) 접속을 차단하는 실험을 하고 있다고 설명한다. 제목과 본문의 내용이 서로 일치하지 않는다.
items.content_ko: 본문은 방문자가 사용하는 브라우저가 anti-crawler 조치에서 의심스럽다고 분류되었음을 알리는 안내 문구다. 2025년 초부터 LLM 학습 데이터 수집 등을 목적으로 한 대량 크롤러가 오래된 Chrome 등의 User-Agent를 흉내 내고 있어 이를 차단하는 실험을 하고 있다고 한다. 최신 브라우저를 쓰는데도 차단되었다면 대학 소속 이메일로 연락해 브라우저 종류와 정확한 User-Agent 문자열을 알려 달라고 요청하고 있다. Inoreader의 피드 수집기는 차단하지 않으며, 그런데도 해당 페이지가 보이는 이유는 글쓴이도 알 수 없다고 한다.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Intel Stock Is Cratering After Trump Poured Taxpayer Money Into the Chipmaker: Did the Trump administration get some bad Intel?
items.content:
In August 2025, the Trump administration raised eyebrows by making a $8.9 billion investment in US chipmaker Intel, as part of a massive $100 billion drive to boost semiconductor supplies.

At first, it looked like an excellent investment as the AI race heated up as Intel saw shares shoot up, reaching just over $92 a share by Thursday of last week, more than quadrupling the government’s initial investment, as Yahoo Finance reports .

But by Friday, the situation looked dramatically different. Intel experienced its worst one-day stock performance since 1974, with shares cratering almost 30 percent on Friday alone. According to Yahoo , that means the value of the government’s 9.9 percent equity stake crashed from almost $40 billion to well under $30 billion, slicing over $11 billion in taxpayer-funded investment off its stake.

Intel’s shares are currently hovering at just over $60, well short of the “NOW $95” displayed in an AI slop image president Donald Trump shared of himself as a day trader in September.

The dramatic swing perfectly encapsulated why the government taking a major stake in a publicly traded company could result in investors being taken on a rollercoaster ride as the value of the Trump administration’s portfolio swings wildly.

Intel’s bruising Friday came after its shares had risen some 150 percent since the beginning of the year, cashing in on the seemingly limitless appetite for AI investments. But the company’s reported Q4 revenue outlook fell short of Wall Street expectations, triggering the major $150 billion market value wipeout.

Nonetheless, the chipmaker still managed to beat expectations in its third-quarter earnings report. The big elephant in the room was the personal computing industry, which has largely collapsed thanks to AI causing prices to skyrocket, suppressing consumer demand. Compounding its PC market woes are supply side production problems, as CNBC points out .

Investors are now divided on whether it’s time to buy the dip or wait it out as the stock swings drag on. Intel isn’t alone in feeling the hurt, with Google parent company Alphabet incurring massive losses and wiping out over half a trillion dollars in market value last week.

Zooming out, Big Tech is navigating a major point of reckoning as investors continue to ask hard questions about its ability to keep the party going and sustain its massive data center investments.

With existing supply woes, Intel is trapped between a rock and a hard place: either pursue a declining PC sector or make a major pivot to data center-friendly server processors, neither of which are a guarantee of future success.

Meanwhile, US taxpayers are along for the ride as the value of the Trump administration’s major investments in Intel continue to fluctuate wildly.

items.title: If you love a website, back it up
items.content:
This story starts with a little tragedy. See, I’ve got these old webpages I love to go back and look on every now and then. There’s websites that have been online unchanged for years and years, or decades, and there’s something a little cozy about checking in on them every now and then to see an old friend is still doing okay. Sometimes, of course, tragedy strikes.

There was this fansite called teapuppies.com for an old anime series and and toy line called Ochaken . It’s about these cute cartoon dog characters who have tea leaves for ears, each of them named after a different kind of tea. 1 The site had been online since 2004 and had basically not changed since 2005, but it was nice just having it around. Except when I went to visit it a few weeks ago, and discovered that not only was the site gone but the domain is now being used to serve online gambling ads.

I work in web archiving, by the way. Which is to say that I should have known the site would go offline someday, and that I have the tools to have done something about it. I could have archived that site while it was still around, but I didn’t. This post is here to beg you to do what I didn’t think to, and to teach you how.

You see, when I talk to a lot of people about web archiving, they always seem to believe it’s something they couldn’t do. It’s something a big organization like the Internet Archive does, and if you want a webpage to be saved you just have to wait and hope it gets done. But that’s not true! What I really want everyone to know is that you have control over the world around you, you can take action to preserve things and make things better. And not just can , but should ! Don’t just wait for someone else to act - get out there and and make it happen! Got a favourite site? Back it up! Got some information you don’t want to get lost? Back it up! Favourite post somewhere? All together now. Back! It! Up!

All of the tools I’ll be showing off in this post use standard web archiving formats like WARC 2 . You don’t have to worry about any of the technical details 3 , but I’m telling you that because it means there are a lot of really great tools to do whatever you want with them. Here, just as an example, is an entire archived website embedded right in this blog post:

You can even click through all the links, look at all of the images, the works. It’s an entire website right in a post! (And if you don’t trust me to keep this up, and you want the web archive to host somewhere else? You can download it for yourself right from there. Just click the kebab menu and choose “download archive”, and you can do whatever you like with it. In fact, please do!)

By the way, for disclosure: the tools I’m going to mention in this blog post are made by the company I work for, but that’s not because they’ll pay my salary (most of them are free!). I just happen to think these are the best tools there are for personal web archiving.

Option 1 - ArchiveWeb.page browser extension

By far the easiest personal web archiving tool is the ArchiveWeb.page browser extension for Chrome. This doesn’t take much in the way of setup or technical skills, and it works for anything: a single page, an entire website, a social media post or profile. So long as you can see it in a web browser, you can save it. All you really need to do is:

Visit the first page you want to archive.

Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click “Start Archiving”.

If your page has any interactive elements, click on those to make sure all their data loads.

Visit any other pages you want captured in the same collection and let the extension grab them.

Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click “Stop Archiving”.

You’re done! You just archived a web page! Now that it’s all saved, you can preview it and see how it went by clicking the extension’s icon and then the home icon to open the extension dashboard. From there, you can click on your archiving session to preview the pages you…

items.title: What are you doing this week?
items.summary: ask, programming
items.content:
What are you doing this week? Feel free to share!

Keep in mind it’s OK to do nothing at all, too.

I got completely fed up with the direction of tech and cold quit just over a week ago. Last week was just recuperating from years of whatever the fork that was, this week I'm starting to look at what a next career might be while also getting some embargoed blog posts cleaned up I can finally post. I'm not really coding anything of import, though, and that's been very pleasant.

Wow. I don't have these kinds of balls. Hat tip for being ballzie. Best of luck on your next arc.

Any thoughts on where it might be? I'm always intrigued on what former programmer/tech people pivot to.

Tech was originally supposed to be the "temporary" career, so I've got some ideas, but I need to start by figuring out how feasible they are when I've got a family and an established community instead of a lone dude fresh out of college in my 20s. All of them are way more about people, way less about tech.

Buckle up. I did this back in May and haven't found anything better yet, which became more stressful, though in different ways, to be honest.

I poured everything into Uruky and that grew well over this period, but it's at 10-15% of the revenue we'd need. I've started focusing on other products recently, but very few people (and businesses) care enough to pay for well-built non-AI products that are privacy-focused.

I envy your ability to cold quit. I am also fairly burnt out, but don’t have the financial runway to quit.

I am also fairly burnt out, but don’t have the financial runway to quit.

I am sorry. To be very transparent, I spent years getting to where I could "just quit", but every single time I hit a goal of "I need to get at least $X amount of runway," I'd find some excuse why that still wasn't enough. I ended up torturing myself with jobs I didn't like and making sacrifices for work long after I honestly should've quit.

I know I'm extremely fortunate that I can do what I'm doing, but this is also kind of the reverse joke of overnight successes taking a decade: I was successful for a decade so I could be an overnight quitter.

(The fact that I genuinely enjoy computing and programming made this a lot harder; I basically got slow-boiled as tech stopping being punk, scrum became normal, the industry collectively opted for predictability over innovation/that innovation that did happen ended up being entirely about holding eyeballs, etc. For a lot of that, because of my seniority and careful choices, I almost got to pretend things hadn't changed. I just eventually hit a point where I couldn't pretend anymore. Probably a blog post in there when I've had a chance to convalesce a bit.)

Congrats. Some of us are too old to go anywhere else and I'm in that troupe.

Taking a full day off (5:45 AM - 10:30 PM) to run the polling place for my local elections. Also threw together a very simple website to support my project where kids vote just outside the actual election (voting for what kind of party to throw in the park 2 weeks later).

In theory I'm supposed to be writing a design document for work, describing some alternate approaches for storing certain data, but time is scarce and I'm concerned I won't have it written up in time because I'm taking time off to run elections and because my boss is assigning me additional work writing up my end-of-year evaluation (I am poor and slow at writing self-evaluations).

Thanks for your service! This is awesome.

I love having an hour to read the voters pamphlet, do other research, and hammer out my votes right at the kitchen table with my wife.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Supermarket Freezers Across Europe Hit With Another Cyberattack
items.content:
Supermarket refrigerators and freezers in at least a dozen European countries were hit with a cyberattack on Monday, following on the heels of similar attacks in France last month and U.S. military bases over the summer.

Stores in Ireland, Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, the Netherlands, Finland, and Estonia saw their refrigerators and freezers heated to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit), according to a report from the BBC . The attacks appear to have hit a large number of chains, including Ikea, Delhaize, Carrefour, and SuperValu, among others.

A few hours after this article was first published there were reports about refrigeration systems in other countries being attacked, including Germany , Portugal , Romania , and Italy .

It’s not clear who’s behind the attacks, but European officials have said they’re investigating. Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away after the attack in France last month, though it’s too early to tell what the economic cost may be this time.

Among the European countries where freezers have been hit Monday, Delhaize supermarket locations in Belgium and Luxembourg seem to be suffering the most. About 40 Delhaize supermarkets were attacked, according to the BBC, while there were fewer shops hit in Ireland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Finland, and Estonia.

Supermarkets allow their freezers to connect to the internet so that maintenance and monitoring can occur remotely. Early reports suggest that some of the refrigeration units targeted on Monday were made by a Danish firm called Danfoss, according to Reuters, which were also targeted in France last month.

Patrick Lamplmair, CTO at the Austria-based cybersecurity firm Tributech, told Gizmodo that assets connected to the internet need to be checked for exposure to hackers, no matter how mundane, especially if there have been previous attacks.

“Reports point to known flaws in refrigeration controllers that already had fixes, and thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack, said Lamplmair. “There is no data to steal and no ransom to negotiate. A few commands to a temperature controller destroy stock overnight and close stores.”

Lamplmair also suggested there should be some common sense involved in how these systems are designed. “A freezer should never accept an instruction to heat to 50°C, no matter who sends it,” said Lamplmair.

The U.S. military is still investigating what’s believed to be a coordinated cyberattack on refrigeration systems at American bases in late August. Military commissaries in California, New Mexico, George, Rhode Island, and others were affected .

Katrien Eggers, a spokesperson for Belgium’s Center for Cybersecurity, told Reuters that it’s not known who orchestrated the attack on European supermarkets and the culprit may never be known. Eggers said she was concerned about the rise of AI, which has supercharged the ability of bad actors to attack infrastructure and commerce.

“All IT systems are potentially vulnerable, and AI can now be used to successfully exploit these weaknesses— especially by sophisticated actors,” said Eggers.

There’s a heightened awareness in the cybersecurity space that everything is more vulnerable right now. Between Russia’s war in Ukraine and President Donald Trump’s pledge to restart major bombing in Iran, there are plenty of incentives for a host of actors to target major infrastructure around the world.

Ukraine and Russia both reported major cyberattacks on their emergency alert systems Monday, with residents of Kyiv getting “nuclear danger” alerts through an air raid app on Sunday, according to Bloomberg . Russia’s Emergencies Ministry app was hacked just a couple of hours later, according to CBS News.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

items.title: US boy names that became girl names and vice versa
items.content:
Picture a baby named Leslie , Kelly , or Ashley , and you’ll probably picture a girl. But all three names were once given mostly to boys. Looking at US baby names from 1936 to 2025, we found that 42 shifted from mostly boys to mostly girls, while just 12 went the other way. Explore the charts below to see how each name changed and what drove the shifts in each direction.

125 names that moved between boys and girls

The chart below follows 125 names whose use among boys and girls has changed noticeably over time. Of those, 54 meet our stricter definition of a switch from one sex to the other.

Each row is a name, and each tile represents a five-year period, running from 1936 on the left to 2025 on the right. The color shows what percentage of babies given each name were girls, while gray tiles mark periods with too few recorded births for a reliable comparison. Select any name to explore its history on the interactive see-saw chart below.

The names are grouped by how they’ve changed. Some, like Aubrey and Lindsey , shifted from mostly boys to mostly girls and stayed there, while others, like Jean and Ollie , moved in the opposite direction.

Not every name made a complete switch. Charlie and Blake were once given mostly to boys but have become unisex, with a much more even split today, while names like Jamie and Robin have changed direction along the way.

Most names moved toward girls, and girls drove the change both ways

The most common shift was from boys to girls. Using a consistent definition of what qualifies as a switch, we found that 42 names moved from mostly boys to mostly girls, compared with just 12 that moved from mostly girls to mostly boys.

But the more interesting finding is what drove these changes. Think of each name as a see-saw, with boys on one end and girls on the other. A name can tip toward girls in two ways: more girls start getting it, or fewer boys do.

For each name that switched, we compared how often it was given to boys and girls before and after the shift. Of the 42 names that moved toward girls, 34 were driven mainly by an increase among girls , rather than a decline among boys.

Surprisingly, the same pattern held in the opposite direction. Of the 12 names that moved toward boys, 9 shifted mainly because fewer girls were receiving them , rather than because more boys were. In other words, whichever way a name moved, the biggest change usually came from girls.

items.title: Postgres 19 is late, and it's AI's fault
items.summary: databases, practices
items.content:
Over the past decade, the timing of PostgreSQL major releases has become very predictable: no earlier than the middle of September, and no later than the middle of October. This year is going to be different. PostgreSQL 19 most likely won’t be released until November, and it’s not impossible that the project could decide to postpone the release further.

Moreover, this year, several rather large features were reverted quite late in the beta period: UPDATE/DELETE FOR PORTION OF , SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ), and ALTER TABLE … MERGE PARTITION/SPLIT PARTITION were all reverted between August 27 and September 15. While major feature reverts are not especially uncommon immediately after feature freeze, which each year occurs on April 8, it is unusual to see multiple major features get pulled from the release at such a late date. So, what happened?

The short answer is that LLMs happened. All software contains bugs, and PostgreSQL’s code base is large, complex, and old. Our git history – converted from CVS – now reaches back more than 30 years, and the first code was written a decade before that. There’s a huge amount of code, and that code contains a huge number of bugs. That’s always been true, and it hasn’t stopped PostgreSQL from being popular or successful. What’s different now is that it’s become vastly easier to find those bugs. Fixing them has also gotten easier, but not to the same degree.

Between April 8th, 2025 and September 25, 2025, there were 1037 commits to PostgreSQL’s master branch and 724 commits to REL_18_STABLE . In 2026, during the same date range, there were 1443 commits to the master branch and 1169 commits to REL_19_STABLE . In other words, if you look at the number of commits that went into the master branch only between feature freeze and September 25th, it actually declined slightly from last year to this year, but the number of back-patched commits jumped by more than 60%.

It’s possible that some of this jump is the result of committers making more mistakes this year than they did last year, but I don’t think anyone who works on the project really believes that’s the main cause. Rather, it seems likely that PostgreSQL committers were about as conservative in 2026 as they were in preceding years, but a lot more of the mistakes they made were quickly found by LLMs.

And it isn’t just mistakes in the latest release. In the same time period, during 2025, there were 248 commits to REL_17_STABLE , and during 2026, there were 433 commits to REL_18_STABLE . In other words, the number of commits being back-patched not just to the release in progress but also to at least one prior release jumped by more than 74% in a single year. The reason for this is simply that a huge number of people on the Internet are now reporting bugs in PostgreSQL that they found using LLMs, and the PostgreSQL committers have been very, very busy fixing them.

And I think that’s also why we had so many late reverts, and why the release itself is delayed. Two factors are at play here.

First, because so many more bugs are being found now, it takes more time to fix them. LLMs can draft fixes, but those fixes aren’t always correct or compliant with PostgreSQL standards. So, they still need to be reviewed and committed by humans, and those humans have not gotten any smarter between 2025 and 2026.

Second, time that would have been spent reviewing what went into the release got diverted into addressing security issues and other bugs in the back-branches, and so it took longer to figure out what needed to be reverted before shipping v19.

In the end, I don’t think that the delay in shipping PostgreSQL 19 is particularly concerning. It is not a long delay in the grand scheme of things, and it emerges directly from the project’s concern for quality.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: DroidDeck: The Complete Team Interview
items.content:
When I put together my DroidDeck feature for the website I run with Gardiner Bryant, I spoke at length with the people whose work and experiments helped bring it about. Those interviews became the background for DroidDeck Is Bringing the Real Steam Experience to Android , but naturally there was far more in the original conversations than I could fit into a single narrative feature. I wanted to give the complete questions and answers a home here.

Below are the original 87 questions, with the responses from The412Banner, Max, xXJSONDeruloXx, Kimchi and Astro Sky arranged together under each question. I've retained the contributors' own words, including their little detours and differing perspectives. Where a question was left unanswered, I've simply omitted that person's reply rather than fill in the gaps.

These conversations were provided in October 2026. DroidDeck has been moving quickly, and further releases, fixes and changes may have arrived since the answers were written. References to compatibility, features, partnerships and future plans should therefore be read as a snapshot of the project at the time, not as a current status report. Astro Sky has also been clear that he contributed as an independent experimenter whose work intersected with the project, not as a member of DroidDeck's core development team.

The412Banner: These are my answers to the "DroidDeck Feature Article" questions, written in my voice (The412Banner). Technical answers were checked against the live Droid-Deck repos, most recently on 2026-10-24.

The412Banner: Questions are shortened. Each one keeps the article's order.

The412Banner: I grew up on the Nintendo and then DOS and Windows PCs, and I learned how computers work by building my own from parts in my dad's garage.

Astro Sky: I go by Astro Sky. I've been around in a lot of different communities. I'm just a dude who likes working on projects and pushing the boundaries of what hardware can do, getting software running on things it was never meant to run on.

I'm answering from my own experience as an independent experimenter. I wouldn't call myself a direct developer of Bannerlator or WinNative, and I wasn't involved in DroidDeck's internal planning. My work crossed paths with theirs through shared communities, experiments and ideas. Questions about the team's implementation, release decisions and security procedures are best answered by the core developers.

QUESTION 01 / 87 Before we get into DroidDeck itself, I'd love to know a little about each of you. What are your earliest memories of playing video games, and what were the systems or particular games that really made you fall in love with the hobby?

My first memories are of the Nintendo and the first Super Mario Bros. After that came the PC, on Windows NT 3.1 and then 4.0. I played Castle of the Winds, and Gorillas and The Oregon Trail in MS-DOS, loaded from 5¼-inch floppy disks. Around the same time, my father started a computer recycling business in our garage. I pieced together my own system from the parts, taught myself as I went, and got online with those free AOL CDs everyone had. A Voodoo card and a Sound Blaster got me into Quake and Half-Life. I played Counter-Strike while it was still a mod, before Valve bought it and before Steam existed.

When I was 6, my mom took me to toys-r-us and I got a red gba sp with Tony Hawk’s Underground 2. I’ve loved video games as a medium ever since!
