items.title: Ubuntu still has not released patch for Linux 0day RCE in almost 3 weeks
items.content:
Ubuntu LTS kernels still unfixed for critical CVE-2026-98432

No patched kernels are available yet for 22.04, 24.04, or 26.04 despite a CVSS 9.8 rating.

Ubuntu has not shipped fixed kernels for CVE-2026-98432 , a critical vulnerability scored CVSS 9.8, leaving the 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 LTS releases without a vendor update.

Operators running those releases therefore have no official kernel package that closes the hole. The gap matters most for internet-facing and multi-tenant self-hosted systems that rely on Ubuntu’s LTS kernels for isolation and privilege boundaries; until packages appear, those hosts remain exposed to whatever remote or local attack the CVE enables.

Ubuntu has not announced an ETA for the fixes. In the interim, affected administrators are left to decide whether to stay on the stock kernel, apply out-of-tree mitigations if any exist, or move workloads onto releases or kernels that already carry the patch.

items.title: A Decade of Kill Bugs
items.summary: historical, linux, unix
items.content:
On the morning of September 24th 2026, Endcrawl had a brief outage. I'd just typed:

Right away I blamed myself. Maybe I mistyped that number! Maybe my code had a signal handling bug. Maybe I don't understand Unix as well as I think I do. Maybe I'm an idiot!

As it turned out, the outage was caused by a bug in kill(1) .

This is really surprising. The kill program is 50 years old. Its spec is simple and stable. It's probably exercised a billion times a day.

A bug in kill was so surprising that, once I'd found it, I couldn't stop there. I needed to know how this bug came to be, and what had led the programmers so badly astray. When I eventually found the root cause, there was an even bigger surprise. It had led to not just one bug, but a whole series of kill bugs that shipped in Ubuntu 14, 16, 18, 22 and 24 LTS.

This post documents a decade of kill bugs, then makes some recommendations.

Back to the outage. I scrambled to put the fire out. After that came a surprise second fire. By the end of all this I was pretty demoralized. I was ready to accept that I'd made a dumb mistake and ready to get on with the work day. There was this nagging feeling though…

Remember that final scene in Burn After Reading?

"I don't f**king know either. I guess we learned not to do it again."

"Although I'm f**ked if I know what we did..."

What had just happened? Was I about to be hit with a third outage? How could I be sure?

An outage not understood is an outage that happens again. That nagging feeling I had was a call to understand. With a sigh, I put all my other work on hold and started a proper post mortem.

Let's examine the command that caused the outage:

The negative number here is a process group identifier , or pgid for short. A pgid is like a pid, but identifies a group of related processes. By convention, killing a positive number sends a signal to a single process, while killing a negative number signals all processes in that process group.

I was attempting to cancel a big Endcrawl 7k test render. A normal person would have killed one of the processes involved and let failures cascade to the others. But killing the whole group simultaneously strikes me as cleaner.

Process group signaling isn't some exotic operation. You use it all the time. Every time you ^C a command, the tty sends SIGINT to the foreground process group. Interactive shells run all but the simplest commands in a new process group, which among other things makes job control possible.

Process group signaling is in fact an awesome Unix innovation. I love it so much I added it to daemontools , where svc -+h now avoids orphans in a multiprocess service bounce.

At any rate, imagine my surprise when the command didn't just kill those render processes, but killed all processes on the machine save one!

Here's the relevant snippet from procps 4.0.4 , the provider of /bin/kill in Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. Can you spot the bug?

opterr = 0 ; /* suppress errors on -123 */

while (( i = getopt_long ( argc , argv , "l::Ls:hVq:" , longopts , & optindex )) != - 1 )

xwarnx ( _ ( "invalid argument %c" ), optopt );

/* Special case for signal digit negative

if ( ! execute_kill (( pid_t ) pid , signo , use_sigqueue , sigval ))

My initial guess was wrong. There's no underflow or overflow bug with -1490947 .

Notice we're in the unrecognized option switch case. Here's what getopt(3) says about unrecognized options:

By default, getopt() prints an error message on standard error, places the erroneous option character in optopt, and returns '?' as the function result.

Aha. The optopt variable only holds the first character after the dash, not the whole negative pid. When character 1 is subtracted from character 0 we get a pid of -1 . What happens when you kill pid -1 ? Bad things :

If pid equals -1, then sig is sent to every process for which the calling process has permission to send signals, except for process 1 (init).

This ran as root, so the misparsing of -1490947 as -1 killed…

items.title: Show HN: I've updated my Linux System Call website and API
items.content:
Every Linux syscall table in one place, grouped by architecture: system calls for 27 architectures with their numbers, arguments and registers, from Linux 3.3 to 7.3.

Every architecture's table, with the full history of when each syscall appeared and when it was dropped, is also a plain JSON file at /<arch>/syscalls.json , for example /x64/syscalls.json .

Number in NR , arguments in ARG0 to ARG5 , then the instruction. The result comes back in RETURN .

Any kernel release, diffs between releases and more in the API docs .

Entries get added and, rarely, removed between releases. Each architecture page has a kernel selector, and its JSON download records when each entry first appeared ( since ) and when it was dropped ( removed_in ).

Removed entries stay visible: pick "all, with removed" in the kernel selector and each dropped syscall is marked with the release that dropped it.

Everything on this site is read from the kernel source itself. For each architecture, the generator walks the syscall table and the SYSCALL_DEFINE macros of every mainline release it scans, so these are the numbers the kernel actually dispatches on.

It also records each architecture's calling convention, the instruction that enters the kernel, so every syscall table shows exactly where the number and the arguments go.

A syscall whose since equals the first release scanned for its architecture was already there back then, and may be much older.

The short descriptions come from the Linux man pages project , and the io_uring ones from liburing . Whenever the data changes, the site is rebuilt from the syscall API .

items.content_ko: 사이트는 아키텍처별로 시스템 콜 번호(NR), 인자(ARG0~ARG5), 명령어, 반환값(RETURN)을 보여준다. 각 JSON에는 항목이 처음 나타난 릴리스(since)와 제거된 릴리스(removed_in)가 기록된다. 커널 선택기에서 'all, with removed'를 고르면 제거된 시스템 콜도 제거된 릴리스와 함께 표시된다. 정보는 모든 메인라인 릴리스의 시스템 콜 테이블과 SYSCALL_DEFINE 매크로를 스캔해 생성되므로, 커널이 실제로 디스패치하는 번호를 기준으로 한다. 사이트는 아키텍처별 호출 규약도 기록한다. 임의 커널 버전 조회, 릴리스 간 차이 비교 등은 API 문서에서 확인할 수 있다. 본문은 중간에서 끊겨 있다.

items.title: Stop Hardcoding Your Timeouts
items.summary: a11y, practices
items.content:
A developer rant about tools built for one kind of internet

Recently, I’ve been losing my mind to hardcoded timeouts . Silent, arbitrary, unconfigurable time limits baked into tools by developers who apparently have never had to wait more than 200ms for anything in their lives.

Now that coding agents are everywhere, everyone is using skills. The popular way to add them is through packages developed by vercel-labs, and the go-to collection is awesome-copilot , a curated set of skills sitting at 30K+ stars at the time of writing. Except I can’t use it. The repository is too big, and the npx skills installer just chokes and dies.

There’s an open issue about this since February #278 on the vercel-labs/skills repo and no one has responded. I’d be happy to send a PR and fix it myself. I just need someone to acknowledge it exists.

Is there a configuration option? A --timeout flag? An environment variable? No, there is nothing.

The workaround I found? Clone the repo manually first, then install from the local copy. It works, mostly. Except now skills-lock.json points to a path on my machine. My colleagues cannot use it. I also have to update my copy everytime I want update my skills. One workaround creates a lot of other problems.

Then came Docker Gordon, the AI-powered debugging assistant baked into Docker. Useful concept. I was stepping through a container build issue, the kind that requires iteration: tweak, rebuild, inspect, repeat. I’ve never used Gordon but when the error manifested itself, it came with a suggestion to try Gordon and so I did.

Except Gordon has a hard limit: if your container doesn’t finish building within two minutes , it gives up. The session dies. You start over.

A two-minute build might sound like plenty if you’re in a fast environment with warm caches and pulled base images. But if you’re pulling a fresh base image over a slower connection? Debugging a multi-stage build with several heavy layers? Forget it. Gordon has already moved on.

There is no way to configure this. No GORDON_TIMEOUT=600 env var. No --build-timeout flag. Nothing. The tool just assumes that two minutes is forever, and if you need more, that’s your problem.

Developers often working on fast machines, in offices or homes with gigabit connections, in cities with world-class infrastructure. They build tools with timeout defaults that reflect their own experience. And then they ship those tools to the whole world, with no knobs to turn.

The thing is, timeouts need to exist. Infinite waits are bad. Hanging processes are bad. I’m not arguing against timeouts. I’m arguing against unconfigurable timeouts. Against the implicit message that says: if you can’t do this in 60 seconds, your environment is wrong, not my assumption.

This isn’t hard. It’s respect for your users.

I’m writing this from Cairo. My internet is decent, better than many places in the world. But it’s not 1 Gbps symmetric fiber. It’s not co-located next to an npm registry mirror. A git clone of a large repo takes time. Pulling a Docker image takes time. These are not failures. They are physics.

When your tool dies silently after 60 seconds without any way to change that limit, you haven’t built a tool for the world. You’ve built a tool for your office.

And this matters more than most developers acknowledge. The global developer community isn’t located in San Francisco or Amsterdam or London. It’s in Lagos, in Karachi, in Cairo. It’s people on 4G connections, on shared broadband, on connections that have real latency because the nearest CDN edge is 50ms away instead of 5.

When you assume a fast connection, you’re not making a neutral technical decision. You’re making a statement about whose experience matters.

I don’t think anyone is doing this maliciously. I think it’s a blind spot. Your internet is fast, so a 60-second timeout feels generous. Your machines are powerful, so a 2-minute build window seems like plenty.

But please: before you ship a timeout, ask…

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Day 2 - Basic navigation
items.content:
Complementary video: File System Hierarchy

Complementary video: Day 2 Extras - pushd/popd/dirs

Most computer users outside of the Linux and Unix world don’t spend much time at the command-line now, but as a Linux sysadmin this is your default working environment - so you need to be skilled in it.

When you use a graphic desktop such as Windows or Apple’s macOS (or even the latest Linux flavors), then increasingly you are presented with simple “places” where your stuff is stored - “Pictures” “Music” etc but if you’re even moderately technical then you’ll realize that underneath all this is a hierarchical “directory structure” of “folders” (e.g. C:\Users\Steve\Desktop on Windows or /Users/Steve/Desktop on macOS - and on a Desktop Linux system /home/steve/Desktop )

From now on, the course will point you to a range of good online resources for a topic, and then set you a simple set of tasks to achieve. It’s perfectly fine to google for other online resources, refer to any books you have etc - and in fact a fundamental element of the design of this course is to force you to do a bit of your own research . Even the most experienced sysadmins will do an online search to find advice for how to use commands - so the sooner you too get into that habit the better!

Find the documentation for the commands we used so far - demo

Navigate between directories, then create, list, move and delete files - demo

This is a good time to mention that one of the many advantages of Linux is that it’s designed to let you know the system, to let you learn how to use it. The documentation available in form of text manuals, guides and forums is where you will spend most of your time during this journey.

Whereas proprietary systems have some free documentation, you see much more frequently the use of paid customer support to fix issues or find how a particular task can be executed. Although you can also do this with Linux (Canonical, RedHat and SuSE are examples of companies that offer support in the same fashion), this is most likely not the case. And you are here to learn, so…

Which leads us to the famous acronym RTFM . Reading the manual is the first thing you should do when you’re learning a command. We will go through the many ways to obtain that information but if at the end of that search you need more insight, you can always ask a well written question in forums and other communities.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-120091 📢 Source: Temporal 💣 CVSS Score: 8.7 (HIGH) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Temporal Server compiles a Worker Controller Instance module, go.temporal.io/auto-scaled-workers, into its Worker Service, and that module registers a compute provider named k8s whose function is to manage workers running in a Kubernetes cluster. The k8s provider built its Kubernetes client from the client configuration supplied in the caller's request rather than from operator configuration, and building and using that client could run a command of the caller's choosing on the Worker Service host, under the account the server process runs as. Two frontend operations reach the provider. CreateWorkerDeploymentVersion requires a namespace write role. ValidateWorkerDeploymentVersionComputeConfig is registered as a read-only namespace operation, so an authenticated caller holding only a read role in a single namespace can reach the provider through it, and that route does not require a worker deployment to already exist. Execution happens while the submitted configuration is validated, so no scaling decision, task arrival, or unusual request sequence is required. Because the Worker Service process holds the persistence credentials for every namespace in the cluster and the cluster's TLS material, the consequence reaches beyond the caller's namespace to the cluster as a whole. The provider is present in the official temporal-server binaries and container images for the affected releases. The control that keeps it unreachable is the compute provider allowlist, the dynamic configuration setting workercontroller.compute_providers.enabled. On Temporal Server 1.31.0 through 1.31.2 that allowlist does not deny by default: when the setting is unset the check is skipped and every registered compute provider is permitted, k8s included, so a stock deployment of those releases is exposed. On 1.31.3 and later 1.31 releases, and on 1.32.0 and later 1.32 releases, the allowlist denies by default, and a deployment is exposed only where k8s has been added to it. The 1.30 release line does not include the Worker Controller Instance module and is unaffected. To determine whether a deployment is affected, check the following together. The deployed Temporal Server version is in an affected range. The Worker Service is running, which it is in the default service set and therefore in a stock deployment. The effective value of workercontroller.compute_providers.enabled contains k8s, or, on 1.31.0 through 1.31.2 only, is unset; check both the global value and every namespace-constrained override, because an override can add k8s for a single namespace. And authorization is configured, meaning a real authorizer and claim mapper are in place; a deployment running with no authorizer already grants every caller unrestricted access to every namespace, so it has no namespace boundary for this to cross. Deployments that use a custom authorizer should also check whether it permits ValidateWorkerDeploymentVersionComputeConfig to callers without namespace write access. The separate per-namespace dynamic configuration setting workercontroller.enabled does not gate the affected path on any affected release. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-02T21:19:19.927Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-120091

items.title: 'America hates data centers,' new database reveals more than 90% of 10,000 public comments are negative
items.content:
As more and more AI data centers are being built across the United States, the backlash is starting to gather pace. Following the recent news that Amazon canceled plans to build four new facilities after a public outcry, a new website seeks to detail how sour public sentiment on the subject has turned. American Sentiment is operated by Prophecy Gov, an AI startup based in San Francisco, and it has turned 10,202 public comments at 417 local government meetings from 2026 into a scrollable collection of facts and figures that will give data center builders nightmares, revealing that more than 90% of public comments on data centers are negative.

Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers

America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price

GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year

Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible

The website notes that, while public comments don't always match the country's true sentiment, it's clear that the discussion around data center buildouts has reached a "fever pitch" of late. That's something borne out by the data, which takes in 48 states and 417 local governments, with 906 public meetings tracked. Of the 10,202 comments, 90.5% were negative, with just 7% saying positive things about the potential for a new data center being built in their backyard. The remaining 2.5% simply asked questions about the subject. A staggering 73% of meetings had no data center supporters whatsoever. Even those who did support the prospect of a data center being built found themselves outnumbered 6:1, according to the stats.

Predictably, a range of concerns were raised in opposition to data centers, with water use being the most common. In May this year, it was reported that a single AI data center project had consumed 29 million gallons of water. It used so much water, in fact, that local residents noticed a drop in water pressure as a result. A month later, Microsoft claimed its new AI data centers use as little water annually as a restaurant . Beyond water consumption, the impact on local quality of life and the lack of transparency around the project made up the top three complaints. These concerns aren't offset by the benefits of building such facilities, with many people saying that they didn't believe that the claimed benefits would ever come to fruition. Perhaps surprisingly, AI and its potential negative effects weren't mentioned in 4/5 of the comments. Just 21% made any mention of AI as a whole.

Members of the public called out some of AI's biggest players when arguing against data centers, including Google , Amazon , Meta, and Microsoft. Concerns also turned personal, with SpaceX/xAI CEO Elon Musk by far the most mentioned during meetings, followed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Notably, Palantir's Peter Thiel was third, ahead of Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos when discussing Amazon.

At a time when the United States may seem more divided than ever, the lack of desire for local data centers appears to be a thoroughly bipartisan issue. Red and blue counties oppose the prospect at almost exactly the same rate, although rural counties raised different issues than urban and suburban ones. The former most commonly worried about the impact on a community's character, farmland, and property rights. Commenters in urban and suburban areas raised the issues of transparency, government distrust, air pollution, and utility bills more often. Pollution is one issue that has been raised previously — a report earlier this month warned that U.S. data centers could wipe out 15 years of progress in greenhouse gas emissions .

items.title: BYD sold more EVs last month than the US did all quarter, topping 300,000
items.content:
BYD sold over 300,000 electric vehicles in October, a new record and more than the US managed in the entire third quarter.

The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026.

BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark.

To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates.

October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year.

BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units.

According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America.

Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year.

By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles.

With several new and updated vehicles launching with its new Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging technology, BYD aims to continue attracting new buyers with longer range, faster charging, and more tech-oriented models.

While the US is coming off its best quarter of the year in EV sales, BYD’s performance shows how far ahead China is in the transition to electric vehicles.

China continues to lead the global EV market, accounting for over half of all electric cars sold worldwide.

With a wave of low-cost domestic brands flooding China’s market, BYD and other automakers are driving growth overseas in major markets like Europe, South Korea, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America, where legacy OEMs are already falling behind quickly.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Anthropic confirms new Claude Code limits to prevent game cloning — users report Opus 5.5 is also actively blocking reverse engineering tasks
items.content:
Anthropic's recent move to have Claude Code deny video game cloning and possibly reverse engineering efforts has come under heavy fire from the software development community. Hot on the heels of Friday's report on the matter, an Anthropic employee responded to the tweet with the purported rule update with a direct statement confirming that the firm added guardrails to Claude Code to prevent game recreation.

In the full tweet, which you can read below, Addy Osmani says that "[Anthropic] added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against [its] usage policy." He goes on to state that work on original games is meant to continue working, and that Anthropic is iterating on the rules to try and "strike the right balance."

We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.

Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working.

We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way. October 30, 2026

There's no telling what those sentences might be, though given Osmani's choice of words, it's possible that said sentences are indeed what X user Chasm posted a screenshot of: "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original."

In our previous report, we had already linked to recent issues raised at Claude Code's own GitHub repository, comprised of users complaining that the AI assistant was refusing to work on their games or on reverse-engineering tasks. As far as we can ascertain, it appears the game-related blocking is limited to the combination of using Claude Code and the Opus 5.5 model. Should that prove true, then users should be able to sidestep the limitation by calling upon Opus using another harness like Ollama or forwarding specific requests through a wrapper of some sort.

Regarding the blocking of reverse engineering, we have received direct confirmations. The first comes from our own alumnus Jarred Walton , who was trying to run checks on the software he's developing. He notes that such work had been performed with no issue until yesterday, October 31, and that switching to Opus 4.8 let him continue his work.

Walton theorizes that Anthropic may have added a new rule to Code specifically for reverse-engineering. Considering that timing, plus the fact that other reports of refusals all popped up around the last week, may indicate that the company could be fiddling with cybersecurity-related rules in the same manner as they are for video game-related content.

We also received screenshots from a staffer's direct acquaintance, who asked Opus 5.5 (via Code) to try and reverse engineer a product activation, a request that likewise triggered safeguards. Meanwhile, notices that Claude Code appears to block reverse-engineering continue to mount, now with a Redditor allegedly having their account suspended , and then reinstated, over using Opus 5.5 and Reverse Engineer Anything . The company has an ongoing Cyber Verification Program , in which only approved entities get access to the full set of frontier models' cybersecurity capabilities.
